item.title: Intangibles by Origin: Bought, Built In-House, or Acquired in a Takeover
item.summary: The same kind of intangible asset (a patent, brand or customer list) can appear on the balance sheet at a very different amount depending on how the company came to own it. Knowing the three routes helps you read balance sheets, compare IFRS and US GAAP companies, and spot assets that are missing.

sections.heading: The big idea: how you got it decides what you record
sections.body_markdown:
An **intangible asset** is a nonmonetary resource with no physical substance, such as a patent, licence, trademark, customer list or software. Think of three ways to end up with a house. You can buy one ready-made, build it yourself, or buy a whole company that already owns several houses. A house you bought has a clear price tag. A house you built yourself has a messy pile of receipts, and nobody can be sure which receipts created lasting value. A house inside a company you bought gets revalued to today's market price at the moment you take over.

Intangibles work the same way, which gives three routes: **purchased** separately, **internally developed**, and **acquired in a business combination** (buying a whole company).

sections.heading: Route 1: purchased intangibles
sections.body_markdown:
When a company buys an intangible from an outside party, the price is observable and the future benefits are presumed probable, so the asset is **capitalized** (recorded as an asset instead of an expense) at cost. Cost is the purchase price plus costs directly needed to make the asset ready for use, such as legal fees to transfer ownership. General overhead and staff training are not part of cost.

After that:
- A **finite-life** intangible is **amortized** (cost spread over its useful life, usually straight-line) and reviewed for impairment.
- An **indefinite-life** intangible has no foreseeable limit on the period over which it generates cash inflows. It is *not* amortized but is tested for impairment. Indefinite does not mean infinite; it means no foreseeable end.

sections.heading: Route 2: internally developed intangibles
sections.body_markdown:
When a company builds an intangible itself, the benefits are uncertain and costs are hard to trace. Both IFRS and US GAAP therefore refuse to capitalize most of it. **Research** costs (the search for new knowledge) are expensed as incurred under both frameworks. Internally built brands, customer lists, mastheads and similar items are not recognized as assets, and advertising is expensed. Legal fees to register or defend a right can be capitalized.

**Development** costs (applying research to a specific product) are where the frameworks differ.
- **IFRS:** development costs are capitalized once all of the criteria are shown, including technical and economic feasibility, intent to complete, ability to use or sell the asset, and reliable measurement. Costs before that point stay expensed and are not added back later.
- **US GAAP:** development costs are generally expensed. The main exceptions are software, where costs for software to be sold are capitalized after technological feasibility is established and costs for internal-use software are capitalized in the application-development stage.

Consequence: a heavy R&D spender can have a balance sheet that understates its real economic resources, and the understatement is usually larger under US GAAP.

sections.heading: Route 3: acquired in a business combination
What it means for analysis
sections.body_markdown:
- **Comparability:** a company that grew by acquisitions shows large intangibles and goodwill. A company that grew organically shows few, even if its brands are equally valuable.
- **IFRS vs US GAAP:** capitalizing development costs raises assets, equity and early-year profit and moves the outflow from operating to investing cash flow. Later, amortization reduces profit.
- **Revaluation:** IFRS permits revaluing a class of intangibles (other than goodwill) to fair value, but only where an active market exists, which is rare. US GAAP does not permit revaluation.
- Analysts often adjust the statements of heavy R&D spenders to make them comparable.

worked_example.problem: Under IFRS, a company spends the following on one new product in the year: research 300,000; development costs incurred before all capitalization criteria were met 200,000; development costs incurred after all criteria were met 500,000; legal fees to register the resulting patent 20,000. The project finishes at year-end. The patent is amortized straight-line over 8 years with no residual value, starting next year. How much is capitalized, how much is expensed this year, and what is next year's amortization?
steps: Research costs are always expensed: 300,000 expense.
Development costs before the criteria were met are expensed and are not added back later: 200,000 expense.
Development costs after the criteria were met are capitalized: 500,000.
Legal registration fees are capitalized: 20,000. Capitalized cost = 500,000 + 20,000 = 520,000.
Expensed this year = 300,000 + 200,000 = 500,000. (Under US GAAP most of the development would also be expensed, so the 1,000,000 of R&D would all hit income, with only the legal fees capitalized.)
Annual amortization = (520,000 − 0) ÷ 8. On the BA II Plus: 520000 ÷ 8 = gives 65,000.
worked_example.answer: Capitalized 520,000; expensed this year 500,000; amortization 65,000 per year.

formulas.name: Straight-line amortization
formulas.where: Cost = capitalized cost of the finite-life intangible; Residual value = expected value at end of life (usually 0 for intangibles); Useful life = years over which benefits are expected.

formulas.name: Goodwill in an acquisition (simplified)
formulas.latex: \text{Goodwill}=\text{Consideration transferred}-\text{Fair value of identifiable net assets}
formulas.where: Consideration transferred = price paid for the target; Fair value of identifiable net assets = fair value of identifiable assets (including recognized intangibles) minus liabilities assumed. Non-controlling interest is ignored in this simplified form.

exam_traps: Capitalizing research costs under IFRS. Only development costs that meet all criteria are capitalized; research is always expensed.
Assuming US GAAP never capitalizes internal development spending. Software costs are the exception, so the real rule is 'generally expensed'.
Forgetting that a target's internally built brands, customer lists and similar items are recognized at fair value by the acquirer, even though the target never recorded them.
Amortizing goodwill, or treating 'indefinite life' as 'infinite life'. Goodwill and indefinite-life intangibles are not amortized, but both are tested for impairment.
Adding training, overhead or pre-criteria development costs into the capitalized cost of an intangible.

item.stem: A company buys a customer database from another firm for 480,000. It also pays 30,000 in legal fees directly required to transfer ownership and make the database usable, and spends 30,000 training staff to use it. The database has a finite useful life of 6 years and no residual value, and the company uses straight-line amortization. What is the annual amortization expense, rounded to the nearest whole currency unit?

options.explanation: This divides only the 480,000 purchase price by 6 and ignores the directly attributable legal fees, which belong in the cost of a purchased intangible.
Cost = 480,000 purchase price + 30,000 directly attributable legal fees = 510,000. Training is not part of cost. 510,000 ÷ 6 = 85,000.
This includes the 30,000 staff training in the capitalized cost (540,000 ÷ 6). Training is expensed, not capitalized.

item.stem: A company has spent many years and large sums on advertising and product quality to build a well-known brand name. How is this internally built brand reported on its balance sheet under both IFRS and US GAAP?

options.text: No asset is recognized, and the related spending was expensed as incurred
options.explanation: Correct. Internally generated brands are not recognized as assets under either framework, and advertising is expensed as incurred, so the spending went through income.

options.text: An asset is recognized at cumulative spending and is not amortized
options.explanation: This treats the brand like an acquired indefinite-life asset. Internal brand-building costs are not capitalized, so there is no cumulative-cost asset.

options.text: An asset is recognized and revalued to fair value each year
options.explanation: Revaluation applies only to recognized intangibles under IFRS where an active market exists. An internally built brand is never recognized in the first place.

item.stem: Which statement correctly compares the treatment of internal development costs for a typical non-software project under IFRS and US GAAP?

options.text: US GAAP capitalizes development costs, while IFRS expenses both research and development
options.explanation: This reverses the frameworks. It is IFRS that allows capitalization of development costs.

options.text: Both frameworks capitalize development costs once the research phase is finished
options.explanation: Finishing research is not the test, and US GAAP generally expenses development costs for non-software projects.

options.text: IFRS capitalizes development costs once its criteria are met, while US GAAP generally expenses them
options.explanation: Correct. IFRS requires capitalization once the criteria are demonstrated (technical and economic feasibility, intent and ability to complete and use or sell). US GAAP generally expenses development costs, with software as the main exception.

item.stem: An acquirer buys a target company. Customer relationships that the target built itself, and never recorded on its own books, are valued at a fair value of 2,400,000 at the acquisition date. The remaining excess of the purchase price over the fair value of identifiable net assets is goodwill of 600,000. The customer relationships have a finite life of 8 years with no residual value, and the acquirer uses straight-line amortization. Assuming no impairment, what is the annual amortization expense arising from these two items combined, rounded to the nearest whole currency unit?

options.explanation: The customer relationships are recognized at fair value and amortized: 2,400,000 ÷ 8 = 300,000. Goodwill is not amortized.
This amortizes goodwill too: (2,400,000 + 600,000) ÷ 8. Goodwill is tested for impairment, not amortized.
This carries over the target's book value of zero for the relationships. The acquirer must recognize identifiable intangibles at fair value, so there is amortization.

item.stem: A company acquires a target whose well-known trademark was developed internally and never appeared on the target's balance sheet. The trademark arises from legal rights. How does the acquirer report it in its consolidated statements?

options.text: It is not recognized, because the target developed it internally
options.explanation: This applies the internally developed rule to the acquirer. For the acquirer the trademark is an acquired asset, so the target's lack of recognition is irrelevant.

options.text: It is recognized at fair value as an identifiable asset, separate from goodwill
options.explanation: Correct. An intangible that arises from legal or contractual rights, or can be separated and sold, is recognized separately at fair value in the acquisition.

options.text: It is included in goodwill, and measured and tested with it
options.explanation: Only value that cannot be separately identified goes into goodwill. A trademark based on legal rights is identifiable.

item.stem: Under IFRS, a company incurs these costs on one project: research 400,000; development costs of 150,000 before all capitalization criteria were met; and development costs of 350,000 after all criteria were met. The project completes at year-end and the resulting intangible has a 5-year life, no residual value, and straight-line amortization. What is the annual amortization expense in the following year, rounded to the nearest whole currency unit?

options.explanation: This capitalizes the 150,000 spent before the criteria were met (500,000 ÷ 5). Earlier costs are not reinstated as assets.
This capitalizes all 900,000 of project spending, including research (900,000 ÷ 5). Research is always expensed.
Only the 350,000 incurred after the criteria were met is capitalized. 350,000 ÷ 5 = 70,000.

item.stem: Two otherwise identical firms each spend the same large cash amount during a year on a development project. Every cost is incurred after the project meets all IFRS capitalization criteria, and the resulting asset is not yet ready for use at year-end, so there is no amortization. Firm A reports under IFRS and capitalizes the costs. Firm B reports under US GAAP and expenses them. Ignoring taxes, how does Firm A compare with Firm B at year-end?

options.text: Higher total assets but lower operating cash flow
options.explanation: This gets the balance sheet right but treats the capitalized spending as an operating outflow. Capitalized development costs are normally shown as investing outflows, so Firm A's operating cash flow is not lower.

options.text: Higher total assets and higher operating cash flow
options.explanation: Correct. Firm A records the spending as an intangible asset, so its total assets exceed Firm B's. The capitalized amount is reported as an investing outflow, so Firm A's operating cash flow is higher than Firm B's, where expensing reduces operating cash flow.

options.text: Lower total assets and higher operating cash flow
options.explanation: This reverses the balance sheet effect. Capitalizing adds an asset, so Firm A's total assets are higher, not lower. Expensing the same cost under US GAAP leaves Firm B with fewer assets.

issues: solver chose B (high): Capitalizing creates an asset, so total assets are higher, and the spending is classified as investing outflow, so operating cash flow is higher. Under US GAAP, expensing it lowers operating cash flow. Firm A therefore has higher assets and higher operating cash flow, but this is not an available option. Of the options given, A, higher assets and higher CFO, is the correct one.

item.stem: For a public company reporting under full IFRS or US GAAP, which statement about goodwill is correct?

options.text: Acquired goodwill is not amortized but is tested for impairment, and internally generated goodwill is never recognized
options.explanation: Correct. Goodwill arises only in a business combination, as the excess of the price paid over the fair value of the identifiable net assets acquired. It is not amortized and is tested for impairment. Internally generated goodwill is never recorded as an asset.

options.text: Acquired goodwill is only tested for impairment, and internally generated goodwill is capitalized if reliably measured
options.explanation: The first half is right, but internally generated goodwill is never recognized, however reliable the estimate.

options.text: Acquired goodwill is amortized straight-line, and internally generated goodwill is never recognized
options.explanation: This wrongly amortizes goodwill. Public companies do not amortize goodwill under either framework; it is tested for impairment.

item.front: How are internally developed intangibles (brands, customer lists, research) treated under both IFRS and US GAAP?
item.back: They are generally not recognized as assets. Research costs and similar internal spending are expensed as incurred. Development costs are the main exception, and the frameworks differ on those.

item.front: Development costs: IFRS vs US GAAP (non-software project)?
item.back: IFRS capitalizes development costs once all of its criteria are met (feasibility, intent, ability to use or sell). US GAAP generally expenses them, with software as the main exception.

item.front: How are intangibles acquired in a business combination measured and presented?
item.back: Identifiable intangibles (legal or contractual rights, or separable) are recognized at fair value, separately from goodwill. This applies even if the target never recorded them.

item.front: What is goodwill, and how is it treated after acquisition?
item.back: Goodwill is the purchase price minus the fair value of identifiable net assets. It exists only in a business combination, is not amortized, and is tested for impairment.

item.front: Can intangibles be revalued to fair value under IFRS and US GAAP?
item.back: IFRS permits revaluing a class of intangibles other than goodwill, but only where an active market exists, which is rare. US GAAP does not permit revaluation.

warnings: 1/8 items have the longest option as the key
